analysis.one_liner: Taxes investment derivatives at ordinary income rates with annual mark-to-market, ending tax deferral and capital-gains-rate advantages.
analysis.headline: The Senate's top tax writer proposed taxing derivatives like wages, but the bill drew zero cosponsors, never got a committee vote, and died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require investors to pay tax each year on changes in the value of their derivatives — options, futures, swaps, and similar contracts tied to stocks, currencies, and commodities — instead of waiting until the contracts are closed out. Those gains would be taxed at the same ordinary rates as wages, not the lower capital-gains rate, and would be treated as earned in the investor's home country to limit shifting gains offshore. It carves out ordinary business hedging, farm commodities, insurance and annuity contracts, and employee stock options.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be wage earners and the federal treasury. Wealthy investors and funds currently defer tax on open derivatives positions for years and pay the lower capital-gains rate when they cash out; taxing those gains annually at ordinary rates would make people who profit from financial contracts pay the same rates as people who earn salaries, and would raise revenue for public purposes. Ordinary savers' retirement accounts, insurance and annuity products, and businesses' everyday hedging are carved out, so they would not be swept in.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wage earners and the federal treasury

how_it_helps.text: Requires mark-to-market treatment: derivatives not closed out during the year are taxed as if sold at fair market value at year end, ending the ability to defer taxes indefinitely on open positions.

Taxes derivative gains and losses at ordinary income rates — the same rates that apply to wages — instead of the lower capital-gains rate, and attributes the gains to the taxpayer's country of residence, limiting the ability to book them in low-tax jurisdictions.
Rewrites the rules for taxpayers who use derivatives to hedge capital assets, replacing a patchwork of old straddle and constructive-sale rules with a single framework.

Protects everyday economic activity from the new regime: insurance, annuity, and endowment contracts, options received as compensation for services, ordinary business hedging, and commodities used in the normal course of trade or business are all excepted.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy investors, hedge funds, family offices, and bank trading desks that hold large derivatives positions would pay more: annual tax on paper gains, at ordinary rates rather than capital-gains rates. Some taxable mutual funds that use futures or options, and their investors outside retirement accounts, would also face higher taxes. Financial firms would bear new compliance costs for delta testing and position identification.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hedge funds and wealthy derivatives traders

drawbacks.text: Mark-to-market means investors owe tax on gains they have not actually received: a position that is up on paper at year end triggers a tax bill even if the position later loses value, which creates cash-flow risk for any taxable investor.

Ordinary-rate taxation applies both ways, and it would raise the tax burden on taxable accounts that use derivatives — including some mutual funds — potentially lowering returns for ordinary savers investing outside retirement accounts, which the bill does not exempt.

The rules are extremely complex — delta testing, close-of-day identification requirements, and investment hedging units — and would require a large body of new Treasury regulations and compliance work before anyone could file correctly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is a genuine fairness fix: today a trader can hold a derivatives position for years without paying tax, then pay at a rate far below what a worker pays on wages. Ending deferral and the capital-gains break for derivatives would raise substantial revenue from the households least likely to need a break. The carve-outs are broad enough that retirement savers, insurance products, farmers, and ordinary business hedging stay out. The serious costs are real but manageable: taxing unrealized gains creates cash-flow strain, and the compliance machinery (delta tests, identification rules) is heavy and untested. On balance the design is thoughtful, though it would have needed careful regulatory work.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced it in August 2021 and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which he chairs, but the committee never took it up and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden, the Democratic chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, introduced the bill on August 5, 2021, during the debate over how to pay for the year's big spending package.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, which was the only action it ever received.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor, and the committee never held a markup or vote; the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy derivatives traders, hedge funds, and bank trading desks came out ahead: nothing changed, so they kept deferring taxes on open positions and paying the lower capital-gains rate when they cashed out.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy derivatives traders and hedge funds

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon and Chairman, Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tax derivatives at ordinary rates with annual mark-to-market

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a markup or vote for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Financial industry and hedge fund trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed taxing derivatives gains at ordinary rates and mark-to-market treatment during the 2021 tax debate over how to finance the spending package

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill drew zero cosponsors — none from either party — so its support was never tested beyond its single Democratic sponsor.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and proprietary trading firms
industries.note: These firms live on derivatives positions; the bill would end their ability to defer tax on open positions and would tax their gains at ordinary rates instead of the 20% capital-gains rate, directly cutting after-tax returns on their core strategy.

Dealer securities already marked under section 475 are carved out, but the bill reworks the straddle and derivatives rules bank trading desks rely on, taxes many of their positions at ordinary rates, and adds heavy new delta-testing and identification compliance. Brokers would also take on year-end valuation reporting for customers.

The bill expressly exempts insurance, annuity, and endowment contracts, so these products keep their current tax treatment while taxable derivatives accounts face the new regime — a relative advantage for the industry and protection for policyholders' savings vehicles.

Contracts on commodities used in the normal course of a trade or business, with physical delivery, are excepted, so airlines, grain handlers, and manufacturers keep hedging fuel and crops under existing rules untouched.
